warmup.text_pt: Um meteorologista diz "**70% de chance de chuva**". O que isso significa? No C2, você vai além de "may" e "must": "**In all likelihood**...", "**There's every reason to believe**...", "It **needn't necessarily** mean...".

grammar.title: Fine-grained epistemic modality
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Escala de certeza com expressões nominais e adverbiais** (do mais certo ao menos):
- **certo:** it's a foregone conclusion · undoubtedly · without a doubt · there's no question that
- **quase certo:** in all likelihood · in all probability · there's every chance / reason to believe · the odds are (that)
- **provável:** it's (highly) likely that · S is likely to · chances are (that)
- **possível:** conceivably · it's not inconceivable that (litotes!) · there's a (slim / outside) chance that
- **improvável:** it's doubtful whether · S is unlikely to · it's a long shot
- **impossível:** it's inconceivable / unthinkable that · there's no way that (informal)

**2. Modais + advérbios** (graduação fina):
- **may / might / could well** (bem provável) x **may / might just** (pequena chance)
- **can't possibly / couldn't possibly** (impossível) — "She **can't possibly have** known."
- **needn't necessarily** (não implica obrigatoriamente) — "A fall in sales **needn't necessarily** mean a crisis."
- **must surely / must have surely** (dedução forte, com ênfase)
- **would probably / would almost certainly**

**3. It + adjetivo + that / whether:**
- "**It is doubtful whether** the plan will work."
- "**It is highly improbable that**..." / "**It is by no means certain that**..."
- "**It is not inconceivable that**..." (= é possível — mais cauteloso)

**4. Atenção ao "no passado":**
- **must have / can't have / might have + particípio** (dedução)
- "**In all likelihood**, the letter **was** lost in the post."
- "There**'s every chance** he **has** already **left**."

**5. Comunicar incerteza:** separe **o que se sabe**, **o que é provável** e **o que é desconhecido**. Evite falsa precisão ("exactly 73.4%") e falsa certeza ("science proves").

rows: in all likelihood, there's every chance, the odds are
conceivably, it's not inconceivable, may well
it's doubtful whether, a long shot, might just

examples.en: In all likelihood, the virus was circulating for several weeks before the first case was identified.
examples.pt: Muito provavelmente, o vírus estava circulando por várias semanas antes de o primeiro caso ser identificado.

examples.en: A single cold winter needn't necessarily contradict the evidence for global warming.
examples.pt: Um único inverno frio não contradiz necessariamente as evidências do aquecimento global.

examples.en: It is doubtful whether the new treatment will be available before the end of the decade.
examples.pt: É duvidoso que o novo tratamento esteja disponível antes do fim da década.

grammar.tip_pt: "**Needn't necessarily**" é muito útil para **evitar conclusões precipitadas**: "Correlation needn't necessarily imply causation." E "**It's not inconceivable**" (litotes) soa mais cauteloso que "it's possible".

common_mistakes.wrong: In all likelihoods, it will rain.
common_mistakes.right: In all likelihood, it will rain.

common_mistakes.wrong: It is doubtful that if the plan will work.
common_mistakes.right: It is doubtful whether / that the plan will work.
common_mistakes.why_pt: doubtful + whether ou that, sem if duplo.
Modal + have + particípio para o passado.

pronunciation.tip_pt: O grau de certeza também está na voz. Em **can't POSSibly** e **needn't NEcessarily**, o advérbio é **muito acentuado**. Em expressões de incerteza, a entonação tende a ser **mais lenta e suspensa**: "It's... conceivable ↗, I suppose."
practice: In ALL LIKElihood, it'll be fine.

dialogue.title: The forecast
dialogue.context_pt: Uma economista dá entrevista sobre as perspectivas para a inflação.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: So, will inflation fall next year?
lines.pt: Então, a inflação vai cair no ano que vem?

lines.speaker: Economist
lines.en: In all likelihood, yes — though I'd stress "likelihood". The odds are that it'll be somewhere between 3 and 4 percent.
lines.pt: Muito provavelmente, sim — embora eu enfatize o "provavelmente". O mais provável é que fique entre 3 e 4 por cento.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: Some analysts say it's a foregone conclusion.
lines.pt: Alguns analistas dizem que é um resultado certo.

lines.speaker: Economist
lines.en: I wouldn't go that far. There's every reason to be cautiously optimistic, but it's by no means certain. A drought, for instance, could well push food prices up.
lines.pt: Eu não iria tão longe. Há todos os motivos para um otimismo cauteloso, mas não é nada certo. Uma seca, por exemplo, poderia muito bem fazer subir os preços dos alimentos.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: And if inflation does rise again, does that mean the government has failed?
lines.pt: E se a inflação voltar a subir, isso significa que o governo fracassou?

lines.speaker: Economist
lines.en: Not necessarily. A short-term rise needn't necessarily reflect bad policy; it could be driven by global factors nobody can control.
lines.pt: Não necessariamente. Uma alta de curto prazo não reflete obrigatoriamente uma política ruim; pode ser causada por fatores globais que ninguém controla.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: And interest rates? Any chance of a big cut?
lines.pt: E os juros? Alguma chance de um corte grande?

lines.speaker: Economist
lines.en: A big cut is a long shot this year. A small one is conceivable, maybe in the second half. Ask me again in six months!
lines.pt: Um corte grande é improvável este ano. Um pequeno é concebível, talvez no segundo semestre. Me pergunte de novo daqui a seis meses!

listening.title: What does "likely" mean?
listening.context_pt: Um especialista em comunicação de riscos fala sobre como as pessoas interpretam palavras de probabilidade.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: In the 1960s, an analyst at the CIA, Sherman Kent, noticed a worrying problem. Intelligence reports used words like "probable", "likely" and "a serious possibility", but when he asked colleagues what probability these words represented, their answers varied enormously. For some, "a serious possibility" meant a 20 percent chance; for others, 80. Later surveys of the general public have found the same pattern. The word "likely" might mean 60 percent to one person and 90 to another. This matters. A doctor who says a treatment will "probably" work, or a climate report that describes an outcome as "very likely", may be understood very differently by different people. That's why some organizations — the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, for instance — attach specific numerical ranges to their words: "very likely", in their reports, means 90 to 100 percent. The lesson for all of us? When it really matters, it's worth adding a number.

questions.q: What problem did Sherman Kent notice?
questions.answer: Probability words in reports were interpreted very differently by different people.

questions.q: How differently was "a serious possibility" interpreted?
questions.answer: From about 20 percent to 80 percent.

questions.q: What does "very likely" mean in IPCC reports?
questions.answer: 90 to 100 percent.

questions.q: What is the speaker's advice?
questions.answer: When it matters, add a number.

reading.title: The science of saying "we don't know"
reading.text: In the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic, scientists faced a communication challenge of unprecedented scale. They were being asked, daily and in front of enormous audiences, to answer questions that could not yet be answered with confidence. How easily does the virus spread? How deadly is it? Do masks help? The honest answer to many of these questions was, at first, "We don't know — but here is what we think is likely." That answer proved remarkably difficult to communicate. Audiences, understandably, wanted certainty. Politicians often preferred clear messages. And when advice changed as evidence accumulated — as it inevitably did — many people concluded that the experts had been wrong, or worse, dishonest. Yet changing one's mind in response to new evidence is not a failure of science; it is the very essence of it. Researchers who study risk communication have drawn several lessons from the experience. First, uncertainty should be acknowledged openly and early. Studies suggest that admitting uncertainty does not necessarily damage trust; in some cases, audiences find it more credible than false confidence. Second, it helps to distinguish clearly between what is known, what is probable and what is still unknown. Third, communicators should explain in advance that advice may change, and why. If people expect revisions, they are less likely to interpret them as contradictions. None of this is easy. A message hedged with qualifications is, in all likelihood, less memorable than a confident slogan. But there is every reason to believe that, over time, honesty about uncertainty builds a deeper and more durable kind of trust — one that can survive the inevitable moments when the evidence shifts.

questions.q: What was the honest answer to many early pandemic questions?
questions.answer: "We don't know — but here is what we think is likely."

questions.q: Why did changing advice cause problems?
questions.answer: Many people concluded the experts had been wrong or dishonest.

questions.q: Does admitting uncertainty damage trust, according to studies?
questions.answer: Not necessarily; sometimes it's seen as more credible.

questions.q: Name two lessons from risk communication research.
questions.answer: Acknowledge uncertainty early; distinguish known/probable/unknown; explain in advance that advice may change.

writing.model:
Will we ever talk to animals?

In recent years, a number of research projects have begun using artificial intelligence to analyse the sounds of animals — from sperm whales to bats to crows — in the hope of decoding their communication. Headlines have promised that we may soon be able to "talk to" other species. How realistic is that?

What we know is this: many animals use complex vocal systems. Some species of birds and whales produce sequences of sounds that follow regular patterns, and researchers have shown that certain calls are associated with particular situations, such as warnings of specific predators. It is beyond doubt that animals communicate, and in some cases in surprisingly sophisticated ways.

What is likely is that AI will help scientists detect patterns that humans would never notice. Machine learning is remarkably good at finding structure in large amounts of data, and there is every reason to believe that it will reveal more about how and when animals use particular sounds. In all likelihood, we will soon have much more detailed "dictionaries" of animal calls.

What remains unknown — and is, frankly, doubtful — is whether any animal communication system is a language in the human sense, with grammar and the ability to express new ideas. Finding patterns needn't necessarily mean finding meaning. A model might predict which sound a whale will make next without understanding what, if anything, the sound refers to.

As for a two-way conversation, that remains a long shot. Even if we could produce the right sounds, it is by no means certain that animals would interpret them as we intend. It is not inconceivable that we will one day exchange simple signals with another species. But the odds are that the first breakthroughs will be smaller, stranger and more interesting than the headlines suggest.

grammar.title: Complex noun phrases and reporting verbs
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Sintagma nominal complexo** = núcleo + **pré-modificadores** + **pós-modificadores**:

[the] [**recent**] [**large-scale**] [**rural-to-urban**] **migration** [**of young people**] [**in north-eastern Brazil**] [**over the past two decades**]

- **Pré-modificação:** adjetivos, substantivos como adjetivos (*labour market*, *health policy*), adjetivos compostos (*low-income*, *evidence-based*), particípios (*the growing demand*)
- **Pós-modificação:** preposições (*of, in, for, on*), orações relativas reduzidas (*the data collected in 2020*, *students attending public schools*), infinitivos (*the decision to expand*), orações relativas (*a policy which...*)

**Dica:** substantivos como adjetivos ficam no **singular**: *a three-year study*, *a labour market policy* (não "labours market").

**2. Verbos de citação (reporting verbs) — posição do autor original:**
- **Neutros:** state, note, report, describe, observe, suggest, propose
- **Argumentativos (o autor defende):** argue, contend, maintain, claim, assert, posit, insist
- **Concessão:** acknowledge, concede, admit, recognize
- **Discordância:** dispute, challenge, question, reject, refute (= provar que é falso!), dismiss
- **Evidência:** demonstrate, show, find, establish, confirm

**3. Sua posição (stance) em relação à fonte:**
- **Aceitando:** "As Silva **rightly** points out..." / "Silva **convincingly** demonstrates..."
- **Distanciando:** "Silva **claims** that..." (dúvida) / "**According to** Silva..."
- **Rejeitando:** "Silva's argument **fails to account for**..." / "This view **overlooks**..."

**4. Tempo verbal nas citações:**
- **Presente** para ideias/argumentos ainda relevantes: "Smith (2020) **argues** that..."
- **Passado** para estudos específicos e resultados: "Smith (2020) **found** that 40% of..."
- **Present perfect** para panorama: "Several studies **have shown**..."

examples.en: Drawing on interviews with 120 low-income families in São Paulo, Oliveira (2021) contends that access to public transport is a key determinant of educational outcomes.
examples.pt: Com base em entrevistas com 120 famílias de baixa renda em São Paulo, Oliveira (2021) sustenta que o acesso ao transporte público é um fator-chave para os resultados educacionais.

examples.en: While several studies have demonstrated a link between screen time and poor sleep, the direction of causality remains disputed.
examples.pt: Embora vários estudos tenham demonstrado uma ligação entre tempo de tela e sono ruim, a direção da causalidade continua contestada.

examples.en: The rapid expansion of private higher education institutions in Brazil since the late 1990s has received considerable scholarly attention.
examples.pt: A rápida expansão das instituições privadas de ensino superior no Brasil desde o fim dos anos 1990 recebeu considerável atenção acadêmica.

grammar.tip_pt: Cuidado: **refute** significa **provar** que algo é falso — não apenas discordar. Se você só discorda, use **dispute, challenge** ou **reject**. E evite começar parágrafos com "According to" o tempo todo — varie com verbos de citação.

lines.en: Every paragraph starts with "According to". And you use "said" for everyone: "Costa said", "Lima said". We can't see what you think of their work.

listening.title: Why is academic English so dense?
listening.context_pt: Um linguista explica a densidade da escrita acadêmica.

lines.speaker: Linguist
lines.en: If you've ever struggled with an academic article, you're not alone. Corpus research led by linguists such as Douglas Biber has shown that academic writing differs from conversation in a striking way. Conversation is dominated by verbs and clauses: "We went out, and then it started raining, so we came back." Academic prose, by contrast, is dominated by nouns and noun phrases: "The sudden onset of heavy rainfall necessitated an early return." Information is packed into long, complex noun phrases, which allows writers to express a great deal very concisely — but also places heavy demands on the reader. This density isn't simply pretentiousness. It allows academics to treat processes as objects that can be discussed, compared and measured. Once "people moved to the cities" becomes "urbanization", you can ask about the rate of urbanization, the causes of urbanization, the effects of urbanization. That said, many style guides now encourage academics to balance density with clarity — and to remember that a paper nobody can read is a paper nobody will cite.

questions.q: What dominates conversation, according to corpus research?
questions.answer: Verbs and clauses.

questions.q: What dominates academic prose?
questions.answer: Nouns and complex noun phrases.

questions.q: What is the advantage of turning processes into nouns?
questions.answer: They can be treated as objects to discuss, compare and measure.

questions.q: What do many style guides now encourage?
questions.answer: Balancing density with clarity.

reading.title: The replication crisis
reading.text: Over the past fifteen years, a growing body of research has raised uncomfortable questions about the reliability of published scientific findings. The concern, often referred to as the "replication crisis", emerged most visibly in psychology. In a large-scale collaborative project published in Science in 2015, the Open Science Collaboration attempted to reproduce one hundred studies previously published in leading psychology journals. While nearly all the original studies had reported statistically significant results, only around a third to a half of the replications, depending on the criteria used, produced comparable findings. The causes of this problem are widely debated. A number of researchers contend that the incentive structures of academic publishing bear a considerable share of the responsibility. Journals have traditionally favoured novel, positive results over replications or null findings, thereby encouraging what critics describe as "questionable research practices": analysing data in multiple ways until a significant result emerges, or reporting only the outcomes that support the original hypothesis. Others emphasize methodological factors, including small sample sizes and insufficient statistical power. Not all scholars accept the more pessimistic interpretations, however. Some have argued that the replication studies themselves suffered from methodological limitations, and that differences between original and replication findings may reflect variations in populations or procedures rather than flawed original research. These objections notwithstanding, the episode has prompted significant reforms. Pre-registration of hypotheses and analysis plans, the sharing of data and materials, and the publication of registered reports — in which journals commit to publishing a study before its results are known — have become increasingly common. Whether these measures will substantially improve the reliability of the scientific record remains, at present, an open empirical question.

questions.q: What did the 2015 Open Science Collaboration attempt to do?
questions.answer: Reproduce one hundred previously published psychology studies.

writing.model:
Remote learning and educational inequality: a brief review

(Note: the sources cited below are fictional and created for this exercise.)

The sudden shift to remote learning during the COVID-19 pandemic has generated a substantial body of research on its consequences for educational inequality. Much of this literature points in a similar direction, although important disagreements remain regarding both the scale and the duration of the effects.

Drawing on national assessment data from over 3,000 public schools, Almeida and Rocha (2022) contend that the prolonged closure of schools in low-income urban areas resulted in significant learning losses, particularly in mathematics. Crucially, they demonstrate that these losses were considerably smaller in schools with pre-existing digital infrastructure, suggesting that access to technology acted as a key mediating factor.

This interpretation is broadly supported by Nunes (2023), whose qualitative study of teachers in rural Pernambuco highlights the practical barriers faced by families without reliable internet connections. Nunes acknowledges, however, that the small size of her sample limits the generalizability of her findings.

Not all researchers share this emphasis on technology. Barros (2023) challenges what he describes as a "technological determinism" in the literature, arguing that the quality of teacher–student relationships and the availability of parental support were more decisive than devices or connectivity. While Barros rightly draws attention to these often-overlooked social factors, his argument arguably underestimates the extent to which digital exclusion itself constrained such relationships during the pandemic.

Taken together, these studies suggest that the effects of remote learning cannot be attributed to any single cause. Further longitudinal research is needed to establish whether the observed learning losses have been recovered, and which interventions have proved most effective in narrowing the resulting gaps.

grammar.title: Complex hypothetical forms
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. As if / as though + formas irreais** (comparações hipotéticas):
- **Presente irreal** → past simple / were: "He talks **as if** he **owned** the place." (mas não é dono) / "She looks **as though** she **were** about to cry."
- **Passado irreal** → past perfect: "She acted **as though** nothing **had happened**."
- **Comparação real/provável** → tempo normal: "It looks **as if** it**'s going to** rain." (provavelmente vai)
- **It's as if / It's not as if** (= não é como se): "Why are you worried? **It's not as if** you **failed** the exam."

**2. Desejos literários e enfáticos:**
- **Would that** + past / past perfect (literário, arcaico): "**Would that** I **had** more time!" / "**Would that** we **had known**."
- **If only** (B2) + past / past perfect / would
- **Oh, to be / Oh, for** (exclamação poética): "**Oh, to be** young again!" / "**Oh, for** a cup of tea!"

**3. Suppose / Supposing / Say / Imagine** com diferentes tempos:
- Possibilidade real: "**Suppose** the bus **is** late — what then?"
- Hipótese presente: "**Supposing** you **won** the lottery..."
- Contrafactual passado: "**Suppose** the Portuguese **had never reached** Brazil..."
- "**Say** you **had** a million reais — what would you do?"

**4. Subjuntivo fixo em contrafactuais e argumentos:**
- **if need be** (se for preciso) · **be it X or Y** (seja X ou Y) · **come what may** · **so be it** · **far be it from me to** (longe de mim...) · **as it were** (por assim dizer)
- "**Far be it from me to** criticize, but..." (ironia: vou criticar)

**5. Contrafactuais mistos e cadeias (revisão B2 + extensão):**
- "Had the Portuguese crown **not** moved to Rio in 1808, Brazil **might well have** split into several countries — and we **would** perhaps **be speaking** of 'the Brazils' today."

listening.title: The uses of counterfactual history
listening.context_pt: Uma professora de história fala sobre o valor e os riscos da história contrafactual.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: For a long time, many professional historians dismissed counterfactual history as a parlour game. The British historian E. H. Carr famously mocked it, and plenty of scholars still regard it with suspicion. Yet, in a sense, all historical explanation is counterfactual. To say that an event caused another is to imply that, had the first not happened, the second would not have happened either. Suppose a historian claims that a drought caused a revolution. That claim only makes sense if we can imagine the same society without the drought — and ask whether the revolution would still have occurred. Used carefully, counterfactuals help us test explanations and resist the illusion that the past was inevitable. Used carelessly, however, they become fantasy, with each imaginary step piled on another as though we could know the consequences decades later. The trick, most historians who use them would say, is to stay close to the moment: change one thing, ask what was realistically possible, and stop before you start writing a novel.

questions.q: How did many historians view counterfactual history?
questions.answer: As a parlour game; some, like E. H. Carr, mocked it.

questions.q: Why is all historical explanation counterfactual in a sense?
questions.answer: Saying A caused B implies that without A, B wouldn't have happened.

questions.q: What are counterfactuals useful for?
questions.answer: Testing explanations and resisting the illusion of inevitability.

questions.q: What is the "trick" to using them well?
questions.answer: Change one thing, stay close to the moment, ask what was realistic, and don't go too far.

reading.title: The illusion of inevitability
reading.text: Looking back, it is tempting to see history as a path leading inexorably towards the present. Empires rise and fall as though following a script; revolutions break out because they "had to"; technologies appear exactly when the world is ready for them. Psychologists have a name for part of this tendency: hindsight bias, the inclination, once we know an outcome, to believe that it was predictable all along. In a series of classic experiments in the 1970s, the psychologist Baruch Fischhoff found that people who were told the outcome of a historical event rated that outcome as considerably more likely than people who were not told — and frequently believed they would have predicted it themselves. Counterfactual thinking is one of the most effective antidotes to this illusion. By asking "what if?", we are forced to reconstruct the uncertainty that people at the time actually faced. Suppose an assassination attempt had failed, a ship had sailed a day earlier, or a vote had gone the other way by a handful of ballots. Would the world look the same? Very often, the honest answer is that we cannot be sure — and that uncertainty is itself a valuable insight. It reminds us that the people of the past were not characters walking towards a known ending, but individuals making difficult choices with incomplete information, much as we do. There is a moral dimension to this, too. If the past was inevitable, then nobody was truly responsible for it: things simply happened as they had to. If, on the other hand, outcomes hinged on decisions that could have been different, then those decisions — and the people who made them — can be judged. Far from being idle speculation, then, the question "what if?" may be one of the most serious questions historians, and citizens, can ask. Would that it were asked more often.

questions.q: What is hindsight bias?
questions.answer: Believing, once we know an outcome, that it was predictable all along.

questions.q: What did Fischhoff's experiments find?
questions.answer: People told the outcome rated it as more likely and believed they'd have predicted it.

questions.q: How does counterfactual thinking help?
questions.answer: It forces us to reconstruct the uncertainty people faced at the time.

questions.q: What is the moral dimension of the argument?
questions.answer: If outcomes weren't inevitable, decisions and decision-makers can be judged.

writing.model:
What if Brasília had never been built?

In 1956, Juscelino Kubitschek became president of Brazil with an extraordinary promise: to build a new capital in the empty centre of the country within a single term. Brasília was inaugurated in 1960. Today, it is so familiar that we speak of it as though it had always been inevitable. It was not.

Suppose Kubitschek had abandoned the project, as many of his critics demanded. The capital would, in all likelihood, have remained in Rio de Janeiro. Rio would have kept not only its political power but also the jobs, investment and prestige that came with it — and the city's later decline, which many historians partly attribute to the loss of its capital status, might well have been less severe.

The effects on the interior would arguably have been even greater. Brasília was intended, as it were, as a heart that would pump life into the centre of the country. Had it never been built, the roads connecting the Centre-West to the rest of Brazil might have taken decades longer to appear, and the development of the Cerrado — for better and for worse — could have followed a very different path.

Of course, it is not as if the interior would have remained empty forever. Agricultural expansion was already under way, and some form of integration would doubtless have happened sooner or later. Nor would Brazil necessarily have been better off. Brasília was enormously expensive, and many economists link its cost to the inflation that troubled the country in the following years.

Far be it from me to claim certainty about any of this. Counterfactuals cannot be tested; they can only be argued. Yet the exercise is valuable precisely because it reminds us that the Brazil we know hinged on a series of human decisions — bold, controversial and, at the time, deeply uncertain. Would that we remembered this when we assume that today's choices do not matter.

grammar.title: Sophisticated comparisons
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. all the + comparativo (+ because / for)** — intensificação por causa de algo:
- "The victory was **all the sweeter** because nobody expected it."
- "Her criticism made me **all the more** determined."

**2. none the + comparativo** — sem mudança (ver C2-M1-L2):
- "I listened to the explanation but was **none the wiser**." / "He was **none the worse for** the accident."

**3. the + comparativo..., the + comparativo** (com estruturas complexas):
- "**The more** evidence we collect, **the less** certain the answer becomes."
- "**The sooner** we act, **the better**." (sem verbo)

**4. Correção e reformulação:**
- **not so much X as Y** (não tanto X, mas Y): "It's **not so much** a problem **as** a challenge."
- **more (of) a X than a Y**: "He's **more of** a teacher **than** a manager."
- **less X than Y**: "The decision was **less** rational **than** emotional."
- **rather than**: "We need to think **rather than** react."

**5. Ênfase com quantidade:**
- **no less than / no fewer than** (ênfase no número grande): "**No fewer than** 40 studies have confirmed it."
- **no more than** (ênfase no número pequeno): "It took **no more than** five minutes."
- **nothing short of** (nada menos que): "The result was **nothing short of** miraculous."

**6. Igualdade e proporção:**
- **every bit as + adj + as** (tão... quanto, enfático): "She's **every bit as** capable **as** he is."
- **nowhere near / nothing like as + adj + as** (nem de longe tão...): "It's **nowhere near as** easy **as** it looks."
- **twice / three times as likely to**: "People are **twice as likely to** remember a story **as** a statistic."
- **by far / far and away** + superlativo: "**by far the most** common bias"

grammar.tip_pt: "**Not so much X as Y**" é perfeita para **corrigir** uma interpretação comum — ótima em redações C2: "The issue is **not so much** technological **as** political." E "**all the more**" vem quase sempre seguido de **because / for / given**.

common_mistakes.wrong: It was the more impressive because she was ill.
common_mistakes.right: It was all the more impressive because she was ill.
common_mistakes.why_pt: A estrutura é all the + comparativo.

common_mistakes.wrong: It's not so much a problem but a challenge.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Em comparações enfáticas, acentue os **elementos contrastados**: "not so much a PROBlem as a CHALlenge"; "every BIT as good"; "NOwhere NEAR as easy". Em "the more..., the less...", as duas partes têm ritmo **paralelo**.

dialogue.title: Why did we make that decision?
dialogue.context_pt: Dois sócios fazem uma análise retrospectiva de um projeto que fracassou.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.en: We need to understand why we kept investing in the app for so long. We lost no less than two million reais.
lines.pt: Precisamos entender por que continuamos investindo no app por tanto tempo. Perdemos nada menos que dois milhões de reais.

lines.speaker: Carol
lines.en: Honestly? It wasn't so much a business decision as an emotional one. We'd already put so much in that stopping felt like admitting failure.
lines.pt: Sinceramente? Não foi tanto uma decisão de negócios, mas emocional. Já tínhamos colocado tanto que parar parecia admitir o fracasso.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.en: The sunk cost fallacy, in other words. And the more we spent, the harder it was to walk away.
lines.pt: A falácia do custo afundado, em outras palavras. E quanto mais gastávamos, mais difícil era desistir.

lines.speaker: Carol
lines.en: And confirmation bias. Every small piece of good news made us all the more convinced we were right, and we ignored the bad numbers.
lines.pt: E viés de confirmação. Cada pequena notícia boa nos deixava ainda mais convencidos de que estávamos certos, e ignorávamos os números ruins.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.en: The consultant's report was clear, too. I read it three times and was none the wiser — or rather, I didn't want to be.
lines.pt: O relatório do consultor também era claro. Li três vezes e não entendi nada a mais — ou melhor, eu não queria entender.

lines.speaker: Carol
lines.en: At least we're learning from it. Our next project will be every bit as ambitious, but with clear rules for when to stop.
lines.pt: Pelo menos estamos aprendendo. Nosso próximo projeto vai ser tão ambicioso quanto, mas com regras claras para quando parar.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.en: Agreed. Let's decide the exit criteria before we start — when we're nowhere near as emotionally involved.
lines.pt: Concordo. Vamos decidir os critérios de saída antes de começar — quando não estivermos nem de longe tão envolvidos emocionalmente.

listening.title: Two systems of thinking
listening.context_pt: Uma psicóloga explica a ideia dos "dois sistemas" de Daniel Kahneman.

lines.speaker: Psychologist
lines.en: In his best-selling book Thinking, Fast and Slow, the psychologist Daniel Kahneman, who won the Nobel Prize in economics in 2002, popularized a useful way of describing the mind. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive: it recognizes a face, reads a simple sentence, or tells you instantly that two plus two is four. System 2 is slow, effortful and deliberate: it's what you use to calculate 17 times 24 or fill in a tax form. Most of the time, System 1 serves us well. The problem is that it's not so much accurate as confident. It jumps to conclusions, relies on rules of thumb and is easily influenced by irrelevant information — a number you saw a minute ago, for example, can affect your estimate of something completely unrelated. That's called anchoring. System 2 can correct these errors, but it's lazy; it takes effort, and we're often happy to accept the first answer that comes to mind. The lesson isn't that intuition is useless. It's that, the higher the stakes, the more it pays to slow down.

questions.q: How is System 1 described?
questions.answer: Fast, automatic and intuitive.

questions.q: How is System 2 described?
questions.answer: Slow, effortful and deliberate.

questions.q: What is anchoring?
questions.answer: Being influenced by an irrelevant number when making an estimate.

questions.q: What is the speaker's lesson?
questions.answer: The higher the stakes, the more it pays to slow down.

reading.title: The expert's blind spot
reading.text: It is natural to assume that expertise protects us from error. The more we know about a subject, surely, the better our judgements become. In many domains, this is true: an experienced radiologist is far more likely to spot a tumour than a beginner, and a chess grandmaster sees patterns invisible to a novice. Yet research on expert judgement offers a more complicated picture. In a famous long-term study, the political scientist Philip Tetlock collected thousands of predictions from experts in politics and economics over many years. When he compared their forecasts with what actually happened, the results were sobering. Many experts performed only slightly better than chance, and in some cases no better than simple statistical rules. Strikingly, the most famous experts — those most often quoted in the media — were often among the least accurate. Tetlock drew on an image from the philosopher Isaiah Berlin to explain the difference. "Hedgehogs" know one big thing: they view the world through a single theory and make bold, confident predictions. "Foxes" know many small things: they draw on multiple perspectives, are comfortable with uncertainty and readily change their minds. On average, foxes made more accurate forecasts. Hedgehogs, however, were all the more appealing to audiences precisely because of their confidence. The lesson is not so much that experts are useless as that confidence and accuracy are by no means the same thing. Indeed, the Dunning–Kruger effect — the finding that people with limited knowledge in a field tend to overestimate their competence — suggests that confidence can sometimes be a sign of ignorance rather than mastery. The best thinkers, it seems, are every bit as knowledgeable as the boldest ones, but nowhere near as certain. For those of us who listen to experts, the implication is clear: be wary of anyone who is never in doubt.

questions.q: What did Tetlock's study involve?
questions.answer: Collecting thousands of expert predictions over many years and comparing them with what happened.

questions.q: What was surprising about the most famous experts?
questions.answer: They were often among the least accurate.

questions.q: What is the difference between "hedgehogs" and "foxes"?
questions.answer: Hedgehogs know one big thing and are confident; foxes know many things, accept uncertainty and change their minds.

questions.q: What is the main lesson of the text?
questions.answer: Confidence and accuracy are not the same; be wary of people who are never in doubt.

writing.task: Write an opinion article (300–350 words): "Should we trust experts?" Discuss the strengths and limits of expert judgement, refer to cognitive biases and reach a nuanced conclusion. Use at least eight sophisticated comparison structures.

writing.model:
Should we trust experts?

In recent years, "trust the experts" has become both a rallying cry and an object of ridicule. For some, experts are our best defence against misinformation; for others, they are an arrogant elite whose predictions are frequently wrong. The truth, I would argue, is not so much somewhere in the middle as more interesting than either position allows.

Let us begin with what experts do well. In fields with clear rules and rapid feedback — medicine, engineering, chess — expertise is nothing short of essential. A trained surgeon is not merely somewhat better than an amateur; she is incomparably better. To dismiss such knowledge would be every bit as foolish as refusing to use a map because maps occasionally contain errors.

The picture becomes far murkier, however, when experts attempt to predict complex systems such as economies or elections. Here, research suggests, expert forecasts are often nowhere near as accurate as their confident tone implies. Ironically, the more famous the expert, the more likely he or she is to make bold predictions — and bold predictions are, by definition, the ones most likely to fail.

Part of the problem lies in the biases that affect us all. Experts are no less vulnerable to confirmation bias than anyone else; indeed, their reputations may make them all the more reluctant to admit mistakes. Overconfidence, too, is less a sign of deep knowledge than of a failure to appreciate uncertainty.

So should we trust experts? Yes — but selectively and intelligently. We should trust them far more in areas where their knowledge can be tested than in areas of pure speculation. We should value those who acknowledge uncertainty over those who never express doubt. And we should judge them by their track record rather than their fame.

Ultimately, trusting experts is less a matter of faith than of judgement. The question is not whether to listen to them, but how.

culture_note.title: Kahneman e a economia comportamental
culture_note.text_pt: O psicólogo israelense-americano **Daniel Kahneman** (1934–2024) ganhou o **Prêmio Nobel de Economia** em 2002 por seu trabalho com **Amos Tversky** sobre como as pessoas tomam decisões sob incerteza. Seus estudos fundaram a **economia comportamental**, que hoje influencia políticas públicas no mundo todo — incluindo os chamados **"nudges"**, pequenos empurrões para melhores escolhas.
